For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the infant Formula Powder came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-infant-formula-powder" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-infant-formula-powder-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of infant formula powder, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>37</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>ASAR 2023</td><td>9</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Dabeka et al. 1987</td><td>2</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Eticha et al. 2018</td><td>1</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Khatibi et al. 2024</td><td>14</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Kuznetsova et al. 2019</td><td>7</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Meng et al. 2023</td><td>1</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Rahati et al. 2026</td><td>4</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>Sipahi et al. 2014</td><td>1</td><td>10%</td></tr><tr><td>State et al. 2021</td><td>2</td><td>10%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for infant formula powder, powder or ground on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>10 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach infant Formula Powder

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach infant Formula Powder comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Infant Formula Powder, powder or ground from Raw had CrIII higher at 2.72 µg/kg, against 2.51 µg/kg for Hot plate in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Saraiva M, Chekri R, Guérin T, Sloth JJ, Jitaru P · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france">Chromium speciation analysis in raw and cooked milk and meat samples by species-specific isotope dilution and HPLC-ICP-MS</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Additives &amp; Contaminants Part A 38(2):304-314</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Saraiva M, Chekri R, Guérin T, Sloth JJ, Jitaru P · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france">Chromium speciation analysis in raw and cooked milk and meat samples by species-specific isotope dilution and HPLC-ICP-MS</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Additives &amp; Contaminants Part A 38(2):304-314</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/saraiva2021-chromium-speciation-milk-meat-cooking-france">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-infant-formula-powder" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-infant-formula-powder" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in infant Formula Powder?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in infant Formula Powder?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, infant Formula Powder, powder or ground had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (0.25 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (23 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For inorganic arsenic, the lowest regional median was in PAHO (0.93 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (8 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
